texts.0: SP, due to a late power reduction combined with an incomplete instrument cross-check, did not maintain the traffic pattern altitude published in the LAP. Altitude excursions exceeded 300 feet on downwind and continued to diverge on the base leg. The IP had to take the controls to re-establish the aircraft on pattern altitude before the aircraft became a factor to other traffic.
texts.1: SP, due to an instrument cross-check that stayed outside the cockpit while maneuvering, did not hold the pattern altitude of the LAP. Deviations reached the 300 foot limit on downwind and base and were arrested only after repeated verbal altitude calls from the IP. SP did not detect the trend without prompting at any point of the circuit.
texts.2: SP, due to trim not being refined after the level-off at pattern altitude, allowed the altitude to drift while flying the pattern legs. Deviations stayed between 150 and 300 feet, SP identified them on the altimeter and returned the aircraft to pattern altitude in time and without any IP intervention. The remaining legs were flown on altitude.
texts.3: SP maintained the traffic pattern altitude of the LAP within 150 feet throughout the circuit, on every leg and during the turns. SP trimmed the aircraft after the level-off and corrected the small deviations that appeared immediately, using precise and smooth control and power inputs. The altitude cross-check ran continuously in parallel with the lookout.
texts.4: SP flew the whole traffic pattern with altitude deviations of only a few tens of feet, well inside the required tolerance. The aircraft was trimmed correctly, the level-off at pattern altitude was accurate and altitude was preserved unchanged through the turns and the configuration changes. Corrections were anticipatory rather than reactive.
texts.marginal: SP kept the pattern altitude within standards, but this axis was marginal: deviations repeatedly approached 150 feet, with a consistent tendency to descend below the LAP pattern altitude during the downwind and base turns. Corrections were correct but were applied after the deviation had developed rather than at its onset. SP is expected to anticipate the altitude loss in the turns and to hold the pattern altitude with a clearly narrower margin in the following sorties.

texts_at.1: SP returned to the LAP pattern altitude with the deviation at about 280 feet before the following leg was reached. The late correction traced to the altitude cross-check being carried out with attention mostly outside the cockpit while manoeuvring. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to keep the altimeter in the cross-check while manoeuvring, from the first turn of the circuit.
texts_at.2: SP identified the deviation on the altimeter and returned to pattern altitude in time, holding the excursion to about 210 feet. The drift traced to trim not being refined again after the level-off at pattern altitude. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to refine the trim again shortly after every level-off at pattern altitude, not rely on the initial trim setting.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the traffic pattern altitude of the LAP within about 95 feet throughout the circuit, small deviations corrected immediately with smooth control and power inputs. The small residual came from a correction applied a moment after the trend first appeared rather than at its onset. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the correction at the first indication of the trend rather than a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP kept the altimeter in the cross-check while manoeuvring and corrected any developing drift before it grew, holding altitude to about 205 feet of the LAP pattern altitude. Applying that correction at the first indication of the trend, on every leg, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good pattern altitude control.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the traffic pattern altitude of the LAP within about 95 feet throughout the circuit, on every leg and during the turns, trimming the aircraft after the level-off and correcting small deviations immediately. The technique is already sound; only the turn onto base still calls for the cross-check to be a shade tighter. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good pattern altitude discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew the whole traffic pattern with altitude deviations of only about 30 feet, well inside the required tolerance, trimmed correctly with the level-off accurate and altitude preserved unchanged through the turns. The only refinement available was to log the level-off technique for the debrief, since altitude control itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent pattern altitude control.

texts.0: SP, due to power management that lagged behind the configuration changes, did not stabilize the aircraft on the airspeeds prescribed for the traffic pattern. Deviations exceeded 20 knots on downwind and grew further during the base turn, leaving the aircraft fast and displaced from the pattern. The IP had to intervene on the throttle and the controls to bring the aircraft back to the correct pattern speed.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed retrimming after each configuration change, did not hold the pattern airspeeds of the LAP. Deviations reached the 20 knot limit and were reduced only after successive verbal power and airspeed calls by the IP. SP did not connect the airspeed error to the power setting without prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a power setting selected without reference to the airspeed indication after the level-off, allowed the pattern airspeed to drift. Errors stayed between 10 and 20 knots, SP identified them during the cross-check and re-established the prescribed airspeed in time and without IP intervention. The remaining legs were flown on speed.
texts.3: SP maintained the traffic pattern airspeeds within 10 knots on every leg of the circuit. Power was set early for each configuration change, the aircraft was retrimmed and the small airspeed errors were corrected immediately with smooth throttle inputs. The airspeed indication was cross-checked continuously against the aircraft attitude.
texts.4: SP flew the traffic pattern with airspeed deviations of only a few knots throughout the circuit. Power changes were anticipatory, the aircraft was stabilized on the prescribed speed for each leg without oscillation, and the airspeed was preserved unchanged through the turns and the configuration changes.
texts.marginal: SP kept the pattern airspeeds within standards, but this axis was marginal: errors repeatedly approached 10 knots, with a persistent tendency to remain fast after the downwind level-off. The corrections were correct but late, so the airspeed was regained close to the turn to base rather than early on the leg. SP is expected to set power earlier for each configuration change and to hold the pattern airspeed with a clearly narrower margin.

texts_at.1: SP brought the airspeed back onto the pattern figure with the deviation at about 18 knots before it was corrected. The late reduction traced to retrimming being delayed after each configuration change. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to retrim immediately after every configuration change, from the first one of the circuit.
texts_at.2: SP identified the deviation during the cross-check and re-established the prescribed airspeed in time, holding the excursion to about 14 knots. The drift traced to power being set without reference to the airspeed indication after the level-off. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to reference the airspeed indication the instant power is set after level-off, not after a drift is noticed.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the traffic pattern airspeeds within about 6 knots on every leg of the circuit, power set early for each configuration change and the aircraft retrimmed. The small residual came from a trim refinement applied a moment after the power change rather than during it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to refine the trim during the power change itself, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP referenced the airspeed indication the instant power was set after level-off and corrected any deviation before it grew, holding the excursion to about 15 knots. Referencing that indication at the moment of every power change, on every leg, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound pattern airspeed control.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the traffic pattern airspeeds within about 6 knots on every leg of the circuit, power set early for each configuration change, the aircraft retrimmed and small airspeed errors corrected immediately. The technique is already sound; only the busiest configuration change still calls for the reference to be made a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed pattern airspeed discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew the traffic pattern with airspeed deviations of only about 2 knots throughout the circuit, power changes anticipatory and the aircraft stabilized on the prescribed speed for each leg without oscillation. The only refinement available was to log the anticipated power settings for the debrief, since airspeed control itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional pattern airspeed control.

texts.0: SP, due to turns started and stopped without reference to the runway heading and the LAP pattern geometry, did not roll out on the headings required for the pattern legs. Roll-out errors exceeded 10 degrees and were not corrected, so the aircraft ended up off the published ground track and off the assigned ATC heading. The IP had to take the controls to re-establish the aircraft on the correct pattern leg.
texts.1: SP, due to a roll-out anticipation that was not adjusted for the bank angle used, did not stop the turns on the required leg headings. Errors reached the 10 degree limit on more than one leg and were corrected only after the IP called the heading. SP did not detect the roll-out error without prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a heading cross-check interrupted by the configuration changes, rolled out off the required leg headings. Errors stayed between 5 and 10 degrees, SP recognized them on the HSI and re-established the correct heading in time and without IP intervention, keeping the pattern leg within the published track.
texts.3: SP rolled out on the required pattern leg headings within 5 degrees on every turn of the circuit. Roll-out was anticipated correctly for the bank angle used, the residual errors were corrected immediately and each leg was flown on the heading required by the LAP and by ATC.
texts.4: SP flew every turn of the traffic pattern with roll-out errors of only a couple of degrees. Turns were started at the correct points, roll-out anticipation matched the bank angle exactly and the leg headings were then held unchanged without any further correction.
texts.marginal: SP rolled out on the leg headings within standards, but this axis was marginal: errors repeatedly approached 5 degrees, consistently in the direction of overshooting the turn to the downwind. The corrections were prompt but were needed on almost every turn instead of the roll-out being accurate first time. SP is expected to refine the roll-out anticipation for the bank angle flown and to stop the turns on heading with a clearly narrower margin.

texts_at.1: SP corrected the heading onto the required leg heading with the error at about 9 degrees before roll-out was complete. The late correction traced to the roll-out anticipation not being adjusted for the bank angle used on the turn. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to adjust the roll-out anticipation to the bank angle used, on every turn of the circuit.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the error on the HSI and re-established the correct heading in time, holding the deviation to about 7 degrees. The interrupted cross-check traced to the heading indicator being checked less closely during the configuration changes. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the heading indicator in the cross-check through the configuration changes, not only between them.
texts_at.3: SP rolled out on the required pattern leg headings within about 3 degrees on every turn of the circuit, roll-out anticipated correctly for the bank angle used. The small residual came from an anticipation set a touch light for the bank angle on one turn. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to match the anticipation to the bank angle a little more closely on the next repetition.

texts_above.2: SP adjusted the roll-out anticipation to the bank angle used and kept the heading indicator in the cross-check through the configuration changes, holding the error to about 6.5 degrees. Keeping that indicator in the cross-check through every configuration change, on every leg, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid roll-out heading technique.
texts_above.3: SP rolled out on the required pattern leg headings within about 3 degrees on every turn of the circuit, roll-out anticipated correctly for the bank angle used, residual errors corrected immediately. The technique is already sound; only the largest bank angle still calls for the anticipation to be sized a shade more precisely. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate leg heading control.
texts_above.4: SP flew every turn of the traffic pattern with roll-out errors of only about a degree, turns started at the correct points and leg headings held unchanged without further correction. The only refinement available was to log the anticipation used for each turn for the debrief, since heading control itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding leg heading precision.

error_modes.label: Ground track over the published pattern points

texts.0: SP, due to visual pattern points identified late and a drift correction that was never applied, did not overfly the points of the traffic pattern as they are described in the LAP. The aircraft passed outside the maximum radius of 0.5 NM at more than one point and the resulting track placed it into the pattern of the adjacent leg. The IP had to intervene and re-position the aircraft on the published track.
texts.1: SP, due to the pattern points being flown from memory instead of being acquired visually, did not fly the published traffic pattern track accurately. The aircraft passed at the 0.5 NM limit at the pattern points and returned to the published track only after the IP pointed out the reference features. SP did not perceive the displacement without prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a wind drift correction applied later than the turn onto the leg, drifted off the ground track described in the LAP. Displacement remained inside the maximum radius of 0.5 NM, SP identified the reference points and re-established the aircraft on the published track in time and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP overflew all the points of the traffic pattern as they are described in the LAP, comfortably inside the maximum radius of 0.5 NM. Each point was acquired visually in time, the drift correction was applied on the leg from the beginning and the pattern was flown with a stable and repeatable ground track.
texts.4: SP flew the traffic pattern essentially over the published points, with displacement that was negligible against the maximum radius of 0.5 NM. Visual references were acquired well in advance, wind drift was anticipated on each leg and the resulting track was identical to the pattern described in the LAP.
texts.marginal: SP overflew the pattern points inside the 0.5 NM radius required by the LAP, but this axis was marginal: the aircraft repeatedly passed near the outer edge of the permitted radius, consistently wide on the downwind leg with a crosswind from the runway side. The reference points were acquired correctly but late, so the drift correction was applied after the displacement had built up. SP is expected to anticipate the drift on each leg and to overfly the published points with a clearly tighter track.

texts_at.1: SP returned to the published track with the overflight close to the 0.5 NM limit before the geometry was restored. The late correction traced to the pattern points being flown from memory rather than acquired visually. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to acquire the pattern points visually on every occasion, not fly them from memory.
texts_at.2: SP identified the reference points and re-established the aircraft on the published track in time, holding the overflight noticeably inside the 0.5 NM radius. The drift traced to the wind correction being applied later than the turn onto the leg. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to apply the wind correction at the turn onto the leg itself, not after drift has developed.
texts_at.3: SP overflew all the points of the traffic pattern as described in the LAP comfortably inside the 0.5 NM maximum radius, each point acquired visually in time and the drift correction applied from the beginning of the leg. The small residual came from the drift correction applied a moment after the turn rather than during it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the drift correction during the turn onto the leg, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP applied the wind correction at the turn onto the leg itself and identified the reference points visually before any drift could grow, holding the overflight noticeably inside the 0.5 NM radius. Applying that correction at the turn itself, on every leg, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady pattern track discipline.
texts_above.3: SP overflew all the points of the traffic pattern as described in the LAP comfortably inside the 0.5 NM maximum radius, each point acquired visually in time, the drift correction applied on the leg from the beginning, the pattern flown with a stable and repeatable ground track. The technique is already sound; only the turn onto the leg still calls for the correction to be applied a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed pattern track accuracy.
texts_above.4: SP flew the traffic pattern essentially over the published points, displacement negligible against the 0.5 NM maximum radius, visual references acquired well in advance and wind drift anticipated on each leg. The only refinement available was to log the anticipated drift for the debrief, since the track itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional pattern track precision.

error_modes.label: Spacing from other pattern traffic and clearing

texts.0: SP, due to a scan that stayed inside the cockpit and the absence of active monitoring of the preceding aircraft, did not maintain proper spacing to the other traffic in the pattern and did not clear constantly. The preceding aircraft was allowed to close to a distance that made the sequence unworkable and the conflict was not recognized by SP at any stage. The IP had to intervene and direct an extension of the leg to restore separation.
texts.1: SP, due to a lookout limited to the direction of flight, did not maintain proper spacing to the traffic ahead in the pattern and cleared only intermittently. Spacing eroded to the point where the IP had to call the traffic, and SP extended the leg only after that call. The recovery was correct but entirely prompted.
texts.2: SP, due to a lookout that was interrupted during the configuration changes, allowed the spacing to the preceding aircraft to reduce below what the sequence required. SP re-established the constant clearing scan, identified the closure without prompting and adjusted the leg in time to restore proper spacing, with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained proper spacing to all other traffic in the pattern while clearing constantly. The preceding and following aircraft were monitored visually and by radio throughout the circuit, and the pattern legs were adjusted early and smoothly so that the sequence was maintained without any prompting.
texts.4: SP kept the clearing scan running continuously through every leg and turn of the pattern and maintained accurate spacing to all other traffic without any prompting. Adjustments to the legs were anticipatory, based on the position of the preceding aircraft, and the sequence was preserved with no rushed corrections at any point.
texts.marginal: SP maintained proper spacing and cleared throughout the pattern within standards, but this axis was marginal: the clearing scan lapsed each time attention shifted to the configuration changes, and spacing to the aircraft ahead was allowed to reduce more than the sequence needed before being adjusted. The corrections were effective but reactive. SP is expected to keep the clearing scan uninterrupted during checks and configuration changes and to adjust the legs earlier from the position of the preceding aircraft.

texts_at.1: SP extended the leg once the traffic was called, though the spacing had reached the minimum the pattern allows before the extension was made. The late adjustment traced to the lookout being limited to the direction of flight rather than a constant clearing scan. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to keep a constant clearing scan running through the pattern, not limit it to the direction of flight.
texts_at.2: SP re-established the constant clearing scan without prompting, identified the closure and adjusted the leg to restore proper spacing before it tightened further. The interrupted scan traced to the lookout lapsing during the configuration changes. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the clearing scan running through the configuration changes, not only between them.
texts_at.3: SP maintained proper spacing to all other traffic in the pattern while clearing constantly, the preceding and following aircraft monitored visually and by radio throughout the circuit. The small residual came from a spacing check made a moment after the configuration change rather than during it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to check spacing during the configuration change itself, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP kept the clearing scan running through the configuration changes and adjusted the leg before spacing could tighten, restoring proper separation well ahead of the sequence being affected. Keeping that scan running through every configuration change, on every circuit, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable traffic spacing discipline.
texts_above.3: SP maintained proper spacing to all other traffic in the pattern while clearing constantly, the preceding and following aircraft monitored visually and by radio throughout the circuit, the pattern legs adjusted early and smoothly. The technique is already sound; only the configuration change still calls for the scan to be a shade more continuous. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed traffic spacing technique.
texts_above.4: SP kept the clearing scan running continuously through every leg and turn of the pattern and maintained accurate spacing to all other traffic without any prompting, adjustments to the legs anticipatory throughout. The only refinement available was to log the scan pattern for the debrief, since the spacing itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary traffic spacing discipline.

texts.0: SP, due to standard phraseology not being used and the transmissions being composed in the air, did not give all the standardized position reports. Mandatory reports for the pattern were omitted, ATC had to query the aircraft position and the IP had to take over the calls so that the sequence would remain clear to the other traffic.
texts.1: SP, due to non-standard phraseology and reports assembled while flying instead of being prepared before the point, did not give the standardized position reports at the required points. Each report was transmitted only after the IP prompted it, and the wording had to be corrected before the call was intelligible to the other traffic.
texts.2: SP, due to a report initiated in non-standard wording, transmitted one pattern position report late and imprecisely. SP recognized the departure from standard phraseology without prompting, corrected the transmission independently and gave all the remaining reports at the required points and in standard form, without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP gave all the standardized position reports of the traffic pattern at the required points and in the standard phraseology. The transmissions were short, correctly worded and made without disturbing the flying of the leg, so the position of the aircraft in the sequence was clear to ATC and to the other traffic at all times.
texts.4: SP transmitted every standardized pattern position report exactly at the required point, in faultless standard phraseology and with no repetition or correction needed. Each call was prepared before the point was reached, and the radio work never competed with the flying of the pattern.
texts.marginal: SP gave the standardized position reports within standards, but this axis was marginal: several calls were made slightly after the reporting point and the phraseology drifted toward informal wording under the workload of the base turn. The reports were complete and intelligible, but they were composed in the air rather than prepared in advance. SP is expected to prepare each call before reaching the reporting point and to keep to standard phraseology throughout the circuit.

texts_at.1: SP corrected the transmission after the IP prompted it, the wording needing correction before it was intelligible to the other traffic. The non-standard phrasing traced to the report being assembled while flying instead of being prepared before the reporting point. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to prepare each position report before the reporting point, from the first call of the circuit.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the departure from standard phraseology without prompting and corrected the transmission independently, giving all the remaining reports at the required points and in standard form. The late, imprecise report traced to non-standard wording being begun before the phraseology was settled. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to settle the phraseology before starting the transmission, not correct it mid-call.
texts_at.3: SP gave all the standardized position reports of the traffic pattern at the required points and in the standard phraseology, transmissions short, correctly worded and made without disturbing the flying of the leg. The small residual came from a report prepared a moment after the reporting point was reached rather than before it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to prepare the report before the reporting point is reached, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP prepared each position report before the reporting point and transmitted in standard phraseology without needing a mid-call correction, keeping every call clear to ATC and to the other traffic. Preparing that report before every reporting point, on every leg, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent pattern position reporting.
texts_above.3: SP gave all the standardized position reports of the traffic pattern at the required points and in the standard phraseology, transmissions short, correctly worded and made without disturbing the flying of the leg. The technique is already sound; only the busiest reporting point still calls for the preparation to begin a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good position reporting discipline.
texts_above.4: SP transmitted every standardized pattern position report exactly at the required point, in faultless standard phraseology with no repetition or correction needed, each call prepared before the point was reached. The only refinement available was to log the preparation timing for the debrief, since the reporting itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior position reporting technique.

error_modes.label: Radio monitoring and traffic picture against ATC instructions

texts.0: SP, due to a loss of the traffic picture while the attention was captured by the pattern flying, did not monitor the radio and did not check the position of the other aircraft according to their position reports and the ATC instructions. Instructions addressed to the aircraft were missed, the readback was wrong and SP had no awareness of where the other traffic was in the pattern. The IP had to take over the radio and direct the aircraft back into the sequence.
texts.1: SP, due to a mental picture of the pattern that was never updated from the transmissions of the other aircraft, did not check the position of the other traffic against their position reports and the ATC instructions. Calls addressed to the aircraft had to be repeated by ATC and relayed by the IP before SP responded and complied. SP did not rebuild the traffic picture without prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to attention drawn to a configuration change at the moment of a transmission, missed one ATC call and lost part of the traffic picture. SP identified the gap without prompting, requested a repeat, re-established the position of the other traffic from their subsequent reports and complied with the instruction in time, with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP monitored the radio continuously and checked the position of the other aircraft according to their position reports and the ATC instructions throughout the pattern. All instructions were received, read back correctly and complied with, and the position of the other traffic was known at every stage of the circuit.
texts.4: SP maintained a complete and current picture of the pattern traffic from the radio at all times, correlating every position report with the visual acquisition of the aircraft concerned. ATC instructions were anticipated, read back faultlessly and executed without any degradation of the flying, and the traffic picture was never interrupted.
texts.marginal: SP monitored the radio and kept track of the other traffic within standards, but this axis was marginal: the traffic picture went stale during the workload peaks of the pattern and had to be rebuilt from later transmissions rather than being maintained continuously. All instructions were eventually received and complied with, but two readbacks were delayed. SP is expected to keep updating the position of the other aircraft from their reports throughout the circuit, including during configuration changes.

texts_at.1: SP responded to the repeated instruction once it had been relayed by the IP, the traffic picture needing rebuilding before the reply was correct. The gap traced to the mental picture of the pattern never being updated from the other aircraft's transmissions. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to update the mental picture from every transmission of the other traffic, not only when a call is missed.
texts_at.2: SP identified the gap without prompting, requested a repeat and re-established the position of the other traffic from their subsequent reports, complying with the instruction in time. The missed call traced to attention being drawn to a configuration change at the moment of the transmission. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the configuration change before a transmission is expected, not let it draw attention during one.
texts_at.3: SP monitored the radio continuously and checked the position of the other aircraft against their position reports and the ATC instructions throughout the pattern, instructions received, read back correctly and complied with. The small residual came from a read-back completed a moment after the instruction rather than immediately. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to read back the instruction immediately, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP timed configuration changes to avoid expected transmissions and complied with instructions promptly, holding a current traffic picture throughout the pattern with no call missed. Timing those changes to avoid transmissions, on every circuit, would remove the gap entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady radio monitoring discipline.
texts_above.3: SP monitored the radio continuously and checked the position of the other aircraft according to their position reports and the ATC instructions throughout the pattern, all instructions received, read back correctly and complied with. The technique is already sound; only a configuration change at the moment of a transmission still calls for the timing to be a shade more careful. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed radio monitoring technique.
texts_above.4: SP maintained a complete and current picture of the pattern traffic from the radio at all times, correlating every position report with the visual acquisition of the aircraft concerned, instructions anticipated and executed without any degradation of the flying. The only refinement available was to log the correlation technique for the debrief, since the monitoring itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary radio monitoring discipline.

error_modes.label: Descent planning and arrival at the entry point

texts.0: SP, due to a descent started late and pre-descent procedures and checks left incomplete, did not achieve the assigned altitude before the entry point. The aircraft arrived at the authorized VFR entry point more than 300 feet off the assigned altitude and still in the descent, with the checks unfinished and the entry procedure not established. The IP had to take the controls and manage the descent and the entry.
texts.1: SP, due to a descent profile not computed against the distance remaining to the entry point, did not carry out the pre-descent procedures and checks in time. The aircraft reached the assigned altitude at the 300 foot limit right at the entry point, and only after the IP called for the descent and for the outstanding checks. SP did not recognize the profile error without prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a top-of-descent point selected without allowing for the tailwind, began the descent from the assigned area later than planned. The deviation from the assigned altitude at the entry point remained between 150 and 300 feet, SP identified the profile error in time, completed the pre-descent procedures and checks and established the assigned altitude before entering the pattern, with no IP intervention.
texts.3: SP departed the assigned flight area as determined in the LAP and according to the ATC instructions, carried out the pre-descent procedures and checks in time and achieved the assigned altitude before the authorized VFR entry point. The entry into the traffic pattern was made from the standard entry point, following the ATC directives without any misapprehension.
texts.4: SP planned the return and descent so that the aircraft was level on the assigned altitude, fully configured and with all pre-descent checks complete well before the entry point. The departure from the area, the descent and the entry from the standard point ran exactly to the ATC directives, with the entry procedure and the following points anticipated throughout.
texts.marginal: SP achieved the assigned altitude before the entry point and completed the pre-descent procedures within standards, but this axis was marginal: the descent was started late enough that the checks and the level-off were compressed into the last part of the leg, and the aircraft steadied on altitude only shortly before the entry point. SP is expected to compute the top-of-descent point against the distance remaining and to complete the pre-descent procedures and checks with a clear margin before the entry point.

texts_at.1: SP established the assigned altitude with the deviation at about 280 feet right at the entry point, once the IP had called for both the descent and the outstanding checks. The late completion traced to the descent profile not being computed against the distance remaining to the entry point. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to compute the descent profile against the distance remaining before the descent is started, not react once the checks are already late.
texts_at.2: SP identified the profile error in time, completed the pre-descent procedures and checks and established the assigned altitude before entering the pattern, holding the deviation to about 210 feet. The late start traced to the top-of-descent point being selected without allowing for the tailwind. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to allow for the reported tailwind when selecting the top-of-descent point, not after the profile has already slipped.
texts_at.3: SP carried out the pre-descent procedures and checks in time and achieved the assigned altitude before the authorized VFR entry point, holding the deviation to about 95 feet. The small residual came from a check completed a moment after the descent point rather than in the same review. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete every check in the same review as the descent point computation, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP allowed for the reported tailwind when selecting the top-of-descent point and completed the pre-descent procedures before they could run late, holding the deviation to about 205 feet at the entry point. Allowing for that tailwind on every descent, from the outset, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured descent planning.
texts_above.3: SP departed the assigned flight area as determined in the LAP and according to the ATC instructions, carried out the pre-descent procedures and checks in time and achieved the assigned altitude before the authorized VFR entry point, holding the deviation within about 95 feet. The technique is already sound; only a tailwind on the return leg still calls for the top-of-descent point to be adjusted a shade earlier. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed descent planning.
texts_above.4: SP planned the return and descent so the aircraft was level on the assigned altitude, fully configured and with all pre-descent checks complete well before the entry point, the entry procedure and following points anticipated throughout. The only refinement available was to log the computed top-of-descent point for the debrief, since the planning itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional descent planning.

error_modes.label: Formation positioning for BREAK and direction to the active runway

texts.0: SP, on the formation sortie, did not place the wingman to the right position for BREAK execution and did not direct the formation to the BREAK of the active RWY, due to the active runway and the break direction not being confirmed before the entry. The formation arrived at the break point with the wingman on the wrong side and the landing pattern procedures described in the LAP could not be followed. The IP had to intervene, take over the lead of the formation and re-establish it for the break.
texts.1: SP, on the formation sortie, did not position the wingman correctly for BREAK execution, due to a crossunder called too late in the run-in. The formation reached the BREAK of the active RWY at the limit of a workable geometry and only after the IP directed the repositioning and the timing of the calls. SP did not identify the incorrect side without prompting.
texts.2: SP, on the formation sortie, initially set up the formation for a break on the wrong side of the active RWY, due to the wind check being read after the entry point rather than before it. SP identified the error, called the crossunder and placed the wingman to the correct position for BREAK execution in time, directing the formation to the BREAK of the active RWY and following the landing pattern procedures of the LAP without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP placed the wingman to the right position for BREAK execution and directed the formation to the BREAK of the active RWY correctly. The active runway and the break direction were confirmed before the entry point, the repositioning was called in time and the formation followed the landing pattern procedures as described in the LAP.
texts.4: SP led the formation to the BREAK of the active RWY with the wingman placed in exactly the right position and the repositioning completed well before the run-in. The break direction was established from the wind and the ATC directives early, the calls were clear and timely, and the landing pattern procedures of the LAP were followed precisely by the whole formation.
texts.marginal: SP placed the wingman for BREAK execution and directed the formation to the BREAK of the active RWY within standards, but this axis was marginal: the break direction was confirmed close to the entry point and the crossunder was called late enough that the wingman was steady in position only shortly before the run-in. The result was correct but compressed. SP is expected to confirm the active runway and break direction earlier and to complete the wingman repositioning with a clear margin before the break.

texts_at.1: SP, on the formation sortie, repositioned the wingman for BREAK execution once the IP had directed both the repositioning and the timing of the calls, the formation reaching the BREAK at the limit of a workable geometry before it was corrected. The late repositioning traced to the crossunder being called too late in the run-in. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to call the crossunder early in the run-in, not late in it, on every formation recovery.
texts_at.2: SP, on the formation sortie, identified the error, called the crossunder and placed the wingman to the correct position for BREAK execution in time, without prompting. The wrong side traced to the wind check being read after the entry point rather than before it. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to read the wind check before the entry point, not after it.
texts_at.3: SP, on the formation sortie, placed the wingman to the right position for BREAK execution and directed the formation to the BREAK of the active RWY correctly, the active runway and the break direction confirmed before the entry point. The small residual came from the repositioning called a moment after the confirmation rather than immediately following it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to call the repositioning immediately after the confirmation, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP, on the formation sortie, read the wind check before the entry point and called the crossunder early in the run-in, placing the wingman correctly for BREAK execution without prompting. Reading that check before the entry point, on every recovery, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid formation break positioning.
texts_above.3: SP, on the formation sortie, placed the wingman to the right position for BREAK execution and directed the formation to the BREAK of the active RWY correctly, the active runway and the break direction confirmed before the entry point, the repositioning called in time. The technique is already sound; only the wind check still calls for it to be read a shade earlier. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate formation break positioning.
texts_above.4: SP, on the formation sortie, led the formation to the BREAK of the active RWY with the wingman placed in exactly the right position, the repositioning completed well before the run-in and the break direction established from the wind and the ATC directives early. The only refinement available was to log the confirmation timing for the debrief, since the positioning itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding formation break positioning.

error_modes.label: Use of navigation aids for orientation in the airport environment

texts.0: SP, due to the VOR/DME, TACAN and GPS not being set up during the return, did not use them to become orientated with the airport environment when this was required. With the visual references degraded, SP could not establish the position relative to the authorized VFR entry points and continued toward the airport without a usable position reference. The IP had to provide the position and direct the aircraft to the entry point.
texts.1: SP, due to navigation aids tuned but never identified or cross-checked, did not use them for the return and the orientation with the airport environment. The position relative to the entry points was established at the limit of a workable margin and only after the IP directed the selection and interpretation of the aid. SP did not use the available equipment without prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to the navigation aid being selected later than the departure from the assigned area, was slow to become orientated with the airport environment. SP identified the omission, tuned and identified the VOR/DME, TACAN or GPS, established the position relative to the authorized entry points in time and completed the return to the entry point without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP used the VOR/DME, TACAN or GPS where it was required in order to be orientated with the airport environment and used them for the return. The aids were tuned and identified in time, the indications were cross-checked against the visual references and the position relative to the authorized VFR entry points was known throughout the return.
texts.4: SP set up and identified the navigation aids before departing the assigned area and used them continuously to cross-check the visual picture during the return. The position relative to the airport environment and the authorized VFR entry points was established at all times without any doubt, and the aids were interpreted correctly and without any additional workload.
texts.marginal: SP used the navigation aids for the return and the orientation with the airport environment within standards, but this axis was marginal: the aids were tuned and identified only after the departure from the assigned area, and the indications were consulted rather than cross-checked continuously against the visual references. The orientation was correct but was rebuilt each time it was needed. SP is expected to set up and identify the aids before leaving the area and to keep the position relative to the entry points continuously cross-checked.

texts_at.1: SP established the position relative to the entry points once the IP had directed the selection and interpretation of the aid, at the limit of a workable margin before it was corrected. The late use traced to navigation aids being tuned but never identified or cross-checked. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to identify and cross-check every tuned navigation aid, from the first one selected on the return.
texts_at.2: SP identified the omission, tuned and identified the aid and established the position relative to the authorized entry points in time, without prompting. The slow orientation traced to the navigation aid being selected later than the departure from the assigned area. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to select the navigation aid at the departure from the assigned area, not later on the return.
texts_at.3: SP used the VOR/DME, TACAN or GPS where it was required in order to be orientated with the airport environment, the aids tuned and identified in time and the indications cross-checked against the visual references. The small residual came from a cross-check made a moment after the indication was read rather than at the same moment. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to cross-check the indication at the same moment it is read, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP selected the navigation aid at the departure from the assigned area and identified it before it was needed, establishing the position relative to the entry points without prompting. Selecting that aid at departure from the area, on every return, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable navigation aid use.
texts_above.3: SP used the VOR/DME, TACAN or GPS where it was required in order to be orientated with the airport environment and used them for the return, the aids tuned and identified in time, the indications cross-checked against the visual references. The technique is already sound; only the moment of tuning still calls for the cross-check to be made a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed navigation aid discipline.
texts_above.4: SP set up and identified the navigation aids before departing the assigned area and used them continuously to cross-check the visual picture during the return, the position relative to the entry points established at all times without any doubt. The only refinement available was to log the cross-check timing for the debrief, since the technique itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary navigation aid discipline.

error_modes.label: Power setting in the descent to the pattern (20 % torque floor and speed brake)
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, leading the recovery, controlled the rate of descent by retarding the power well below the 20 % torque floor and never used the speed brake as the alternative described in the technique. Engine response at the level-off was slow, so the aircraft arrived at the entry point more than 20 knots below the briefed pattern airspeed and left the wingman with no closure control. The IP had to take the throttle and re-establish the flight on speed before the entry point.
texts.1: SP flew the descent with the power reduced below 20 % torque instead of adding speed brake, and did not restore the power in time for the level-off. Airspeed at the entry point was about 20 knots off the briefed figure, at the limit, and was corrected only after the IP prompted for power and speed brake. SP did not associate the low torque setting with the slow acceleration.
texts.2: SP allowed the torque to fall to the low end of the useful range during the descent before selecting the speed brake, so the rate of descent was controlled by power rather than by drag. The airspeed excursion at the level-off reached about 15 knots, but SP recognised the trend, restored the torque above 20 % and stabilised the aircraft on the pattern airspeed in time and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP planned the descent so that the torque stayed above 20 % throughout and used the speed brake whenever a higher rate of descent was required. Airspeed was held inside 10 knots of the briefed pattern figure and engine response at the level-off was immediate, so the flight arrived at the entry point on speed and in position.
texts.4: SP managed the descent entirely with speed brake and small power adjustments, never approaching the 20 % torque floor. Airspeed deviations from the briefed pattern figure were negligible, the level-off required no correction and the wingman had steady, predictable closure throughout the descent.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspeed inside the required band on the descent, but this axis was marginal: the torque was repeatedly allowed to sit at the bottom of the acceptable range and the speed brake was selected only after the descent rate had already been set with power. Each level-off therefore needed a noticeable power increase and the speed recovered late. SP is expected to use the speed brake first and to keep the torque clear of the 20 % floor throughout the descent.

texts_at.1: SP restored the airspeed above the pattern figure with the deviation at about 18 knots before the entry point was reached. The slow correction traced to power being reduced below the 20 percent torque floor instead of the speed brake being extended. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to select the speed brake before torque approaches the 20 percent floor, on every descent to the pattern.
texts_at.2: SP recognised the trend, restored the torque above 20 percent and stabilised the aircraft on the pattern airspeed in time, holding the deviation to about 14 knots. The excursion traced to torque being allowed to fall to the low end of the useful range before the speed brake was selected. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to select the speed brake as the descent rate is first controlled, not once torque has already fallen.
texts_at.3: SP planned the descent so the torque stayed above 20 percent throughout and used the speed brake whenever a higher rate of descent was required, airspeed held within about 6 knots of the briefed pattern figure. The small residual came from the speed brake selected a moment after the descent rate first needed it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to select the speed brake the instant the descent rate needs it, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP selected the speed brake as the descent rate was first controlled, keeping torque clear of the 20 percent floor throughout, holding airspeed to about 15 knots of the briefed pattern figure. Selecting that speed brake at the first control input, on every descent, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good descent power management.
texts_above.3: SP planned the descent so the torque stayed above 20 percent throughout and used the speed brake whenever a higher rate of descent was required, airspeed held inside about 6 knots of the briefed pattern figure, engine response at the level-off immediate. The technique is already sound; only the steepest descent still calls for the speed brake to be selected a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good descent power discipline.
texts_above.4: SP managed the descent entirely with speed brake and small power adjustments, never approaching the 20 percent torque floor, airspeed deviations from the briefed pattern figure negligible and the level-off requiring no correction. The only refinement available was to log the speed brake schedule for the debrief, since power management itself needed no correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent descent power management.

error_modes.label: Echelon turn discipline inside the pattern entry point
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, leading at pattern altitude inside the entry point, initiated a turn into the wingman although all turns away from Number 2 are echelon unless briefed otherwise, and did not check the side on which Number 2 was flying. The wingman was forced across the flight path and the roll-out was more than 10 degrees off the intended pattern heading, with the formation no longer positioned for the entry. The IP had to direct the turn and re-establish the flight on the pattern heading.
texts.1: SP did not apply the rule that turns away from Number 2 are echelon inside the entry point, and started the turn without confirming the wingman's side. Number 2 was left in a position that required a large correction and the roll-out was about 10 degrees off the pattern heading, at the limit, before the IP called for the turn direction and the echelon check.
texts.2: SP began the turn inside the entry point before completing the check of the wingman's side, so the echelon requirement was satisfied only after a delayed adjustment. Heading at the roll-out was displaced by a moderate amount inside the permitted band, but SP recognised the geometry, re-established the wingman on the outside of the turn and corrected the heading in time without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP confirmed the wingman's side before every turn inside the entry point and flew all turns away from Number 2 as echelon, exactly as briefed. Roll-outs were within 5 degrees of the pattern headings and the wingman held position on the outside of each turn without any large correction.
texts.4: SP anticipated each turn inside the entry point, checked the wingman's position early and flew every turn away from Number 2 as echelon with a smooth, constant bank. Heading deviations at the roll-outs were negligible and the wingman was never required to correct for the turn direction.
texts.marginal: SP flew the turns inside the entry point as echelon and stayed inside the heading limits, but this axis was marginal: the wingman's side was verified late on each turn and the bank was applied before the geometry had been fully confirmed. The roll-outs were therefore repeatedly at the outer edge of the permitted heading band and the wingman had to work to hold the outside position. SP is expected to establish the turn direction relative to Number 2 before applying bank.

texts_at.1: SP directed the turn and re-established the flight on the pattern heading with the deviation at about 9 degrees before roll-out was corrected. The uncleared turn traced to the wingman's side not being confirmed before applying bank inside the entry point. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the wingman's side before applying bank on every turn inside the entry point, not after the turn is under way.
texts_at.2: SP recognised the geometry, re-established the wingman on the outside of the turn and corrected the heading in time, holding the deviation to about 7 degrees. The delayed check traced to the turn being begun before the wingman's side check was completed. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to complete the wingman's side check before beginning the turn, not while it is already established.
texts_at.3: SP confirmed the wingman's side before every turn inside the entry point and flew all turns away from Number 2 as echelon, exactly as briefed, roll-outs held within about 3 degrees. The small residual came from a confirmation completed a moment after the turn was anticipated rather than before it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to complete the confirmation before anticipating the turn, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP confirmed the wingman's side before applying bank on every turn inside the entry point, correcting any residual promptly, holding the deviation to about 6.5 degrees. Confirming that side before every turn, from the outset, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady echelon turn discipline.
texts_above.3: SP confirmed the wingman's side before every turn inside the entry point and flew all turns away from Number 2 as echelon, exactly as briefed, roll-outs held within about 3 degrees, the wingman holding position on the outside of each turn without a large correction. The technique is already sound; only the earliest turn of the entry still calls for the confirmation to be a shade quicker. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate echelon turn technique.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated each turn inside the entry point, checked the wingman's position early and flew every turn away from Number 2 as echelon with a smooth, constant bank, heading deviations at the roll-outs negligible. The only refinement available was to log the anticipation timing for the debrief, since the technique itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding echelon turn discipline.

error_modes.label: Power reduction timing at the Break point
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, leading the pattern entry, reduced power well before the Break instead of delaying the reduction until the turn to downwind was initiated. The formation decelerated on the entry heading, the airspeed fell more than 20 knots below the briefed figure before any bank was applied and the wingman generated uncontrolled closure from the outside position. The IP had to intervene with power and direct the Break.
texts.1: SP anticipated the Break and brought the power back before the turn was started, contrary to the technique of delaying the power reduction until the turn is initiated. Airspeed at the Break was about 20 knots low, at the limit, and the wingman was left with excessive closure until the IP called for power and for the turn to be started first.
texts.2: SP started the power reduction slightly ahead of the bank at the Break point, so the deceleration began before the turn. The airspeed loss reached an intermediate value inside the permitted band, but SP recognised the early reduction, restored the power and completed the Break as a smooth turn to downwind in time and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP held the briefed power until the turn to downwind at the Break was initiated, then reduced it smoothly as the bank was established. Airspeed at the Break stayed within 10 knots of the briefed figure and the wingman's spacing on downwind was predictable throughout.
texts.4: SP flew the Break as a single smooth manoeuvre, initiating the turn to downwind first and reducing the power only after the bank was established. Airspeed deviations were negligible, the ground track through the Break was constant and the wingman had a stable reference for the timed turn.
texts.marginal: SP kept the airspeed at the Break inside the required band, but this axis was marginal: on each pattern the power came back at almost the same instant as the bank rather than after the turn was initiated, and the speed decayed towards the lower edge of the tolerance before the turn was fully established. The wingman was repeatedly left with more closure than planned. SP is expected to initiate the turn to downwind first and to delay the power reduction until the bank is set.

texts_at.1: SP restored the power and completed the Break as a turn to downwind with the airspeed at about 18 knots low before the correction closed. The early reduction traced to power being brought back before the turn was started, contrary to the technique of delaying the reduction until the turn is initiated. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to initiate the turn to downwind before reducing power, on every Break of the recovery.
texts_at.2: SP recognised the early reduction, restored the power and completed the Break as a smooth turn to downwind, holding the airspeed loss to about 14 knots below the briefed figure. The early start traced to the power reduction beginning slightly ahead of the bank at the Break point. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to hold the briefed power until the bank is established, not begin the reduction ahead of it.
texts_at.3: SP held the briefed power until the turn to downwind at the Break was initiated, then reduced it smoothly as the bank was established, airspeed held within about 6 knots of the briefed figure. The small residual came from the power reduction begun a moment before the bank was fully established rather than after it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to begin the power reduction only once the bank is fully established, not a moment before.

texts_above.2: SP held the briefed power until the bank was established at the Break point and reduced it smoothly as the turn to downwind was initiated, holding the airspeed loss to about 15 knots below the briefed figure. Holding that power until the bank is fully established, on every Break, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent Break power timing.
texts_above.3: SP held the briefed power until the turn to downwind at the Break was initiated, then reduced it smoothly as the bank was established, airspeed held within about 6 knots of the briefed figure, the wingman's spacing on downwind predictable throughout. The technique is already sound; only the moment the bank is established still calls for the reduction to be a shade later. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good Break power sequencing.
texts_above.4: SP flew the Break as a single smooth manoeuvre, initiating the turn to downwind first and reducing the power only after the bank was established, airspeed deviations negligible and the wingman with a stable reference for the timed turn. The only refinement available was to log the exact sequencing for the debrief, since the Break itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior Break power sequencing.

error_modes.label: Number 2 break interval and resulting downwind spacing
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, flying as Number 2, started the turn only two to three seconds after Number 1's Break instead of waiting the minimum of five seconds, and did not check the resulting spacing on downwind. The aircraft rolled out with insufficient spacing on downwind and no room to re-establish the interval before the perch point. The IP had to intervene and direct a go-around to rebuild the pattern spacing.
texts.1: SP did not hold the minimum of five seconds after Number 1's Break and turned early, so the interval was never established. Spacing on downwind was at the minimum usable value and was restored only after the IP called for the delay and for a spacing correction. SP had not monitored Number 1's position while flying the turn.
texts.2: SP timed the Break interval by feel rather than by the briefed count, so the turn was started slightly before the five seconds were complete. Spacing on downwind was reduced but stayed within workable limits, and SP recognised the closure, corrected it with a lateral adjustment on downwind and re-established the interval in time without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP waited the minimum of five seconds after Number 1's Break before starting the turn and checked the spacing during the turn to downwind. Spacing on downwind was correct and stable, and the perch point was reached with the same geometry as briefed for the contact pattern.
texts.4: SP counted the interval accurately after Number 1's Break, started the turn precisely and monitored Number 1 throughout the manoeuvre. Spacing on downwind was established immediately with negligible correction and required no adjustment before the perch point.
texts.marginal: SP held the minimum interval after Number 1's Break and the spacing on downwind remained usable, but this axis was marginal: the count was started late on each pattern and the resulting spacing was consistently at the tight end, requiring a lateral correction on downwind. SP is expected to time the interval from Number 1's Break itself and to check the spacing before rolling out on downwind.

texts_at.1: SP restored the interval and corrected the spacing on downwind once the IP had called for both the delay and the correction. The short interval traced to the count after Number 1's Break not reaching the minimum of five seconds. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to count the full five seconds after every Break, not estimate the interval by feel.
texts_at.2: SP recognised the closure without prompting, corrected it with a lateral adjustment on downwind and re-established the interval in time. The reduced spacing traced to the Break interval being timed by feel rather than by the briefed count. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to count the Break interval deliberately rather than timing it by feel, on every recovery.
texts_at.3: SP waited the minimum of five seconds after Number 1's Break before starting the turn and checked the spacing during the turn to downwind, the perch point reached with the same geometry as briefed. The small residual came from the count started a moment after the Break rather than at the instant of it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to start the count at the instant of the Break, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP counted the Break interval deliberately and checked the spacing during the turn to downwind, correcting any residual closure before it could tighten further. Counting that interval deliberately, on every Break, would remove the closure entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable Break interval discipline.
texts_above.3: SP waited the minimum of five seconds after Number 1's Break before starting the turn and checked the spacing during the turn to downwind, spacing on downwind correct and stable, the perch point reached with the same geometry as briefed. The technique is already sound; only the instant of the Break itself still calls for the count to start a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed Break interval technique.
texts_above.4: SP counted the interval accurately after Number 1's Break, started the turn precisely and monitored Number 1 throughout the manoeuvre, spacing on downwind established immediately with negligible correction. The only refinement available was to log the exact interval counted for the debrief, since the technique itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary Break interval technique.

error_modes.label: Number 2 downwind position relative to Number 1's ground track
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, flying as Number 2, rolled out on downwind inside Number 1's ground track instead of slightly outside it, and did not correct for the drift towards the runway. The aircraft ended up under the leader's flight path with no visual contact and with a track error large enough to compromise the turn to the perch point. The IP had to intervene and re-position the aircraft outside Number 1's ground track.
texts.1: SP did not establish the downwind position slightly outside Number 1's ground track and drifted onto the leader's track. Number 1 was held at the limit of usable visual contact and the position was corrected only after the IP pointed out the geometry. SP did not perceive that the tracks had converged.
texts.2: SP rolled out on downwind with the aircraft on rather than slightly outside Number 1's ground track, because the turn was flown without reference to the leader's position. The displacement stayed inside acceptable limits and SP recognised the convergence, moved the track outside the leader's and stabilised the downwind in time without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP established the downwind slightly outside Number 1's ground track as described in the technique, with continuous visual contact on the leader. The lateral displacement was held steady, the wind drift was corrected on the leg and the turn to the perch point was flown from the correct position.
texts.4: SP rolled out on downwind precisely outside Number 1's ground track and held that displacement without variation for the whole leg. Visual contact with the leader was maintained throughout, drift was anticipated and the position at the perch point required no correction.
texts.marginal: SP flew the downwind outside Number 1's ground track and stayed within acceptable limits, but this axis was marginal: the displacement was repeatedly allowed to wash out towards the leader's track before being re-established, particularly with a crosswind from the runway side. Visual contact was maintained but with an unnecessarily tight geometry. SP is expected to set the outside displacement at the roll-out and to hold it for the whole downwind leg.

texts_at.1: SP repositioned outside Number 1's ground track once the IP had pointed out the geometry, visual contact having been at the limit of usable range before the correction was made. The convergence traced to the downwind position not being established slightly outside the lead's ground track from roll-out. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to establish the outside displacement at roll-out onto downwind, on every recovery.
texts_at.2: SP recognised the convergence, moved the track outside the leader's and stabilised the downwind in time, without prompting. The convergence traced to the turn being flown without reference to the leader's position. The maneuver was flown to the standard the Training Section requires at this point. SP is expected to reference the leader's position through the turn onto downwind, not only after roll-out.
texts_at.3: SP established the downwind slightly outside Number 1's ground track as described in the technique, with continuous visual contact on the leader, the wind drift corrected on the leg. The small residual came from the outside displacement re-established a moment after it first began to wash in rather than at that moment. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to re-establish the displacement at the first sign of wash-in, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP referenced the leader's position through the turn onto downwind and established the outside displacement without needing a later correction, maintaining continuous visual contact throughout. Referencing that position through every turn, on every recovery, would tighten the margin further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured downwind position discipline.
texts_above.3: SP established the downwind slightly outside Number 1's ground track as described in the technique, with continuous visual contact on the leader maintained throughout, the lateral displacement held steady and the turn to the perch point flown from the correct position. The technique is already sound; only a crosswind from the runway side still calls for the displacement to be re-established a shade sooner. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined downwind position technique.
texts_above.4: SP rolled out on downwind precisely outside Number 1's ground track and held that displacement without variation for the whole leg, visual contact with the leader maintained throughout and drift anticipated. The only refinement available was to log the displacement held for the debrief, since the technique itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate downwind position technique.

error_modes.label: Following a poorly flown pattern instead of going around
error_modes.source: technique:9.40.1 FORMATION RECOVERY - DESCENT TO VFR PATTERN, BREAK AND LANDING

texts.0: SP, flying as Number 2, followed a poorly flown pattern from the leader rather than going around as the technique requires, and continued to match a track and a spacing that were already wrong. The aircraft was carried outside the pattern parameters by more than the permitted margins and arrived at the perch point with no acceptable solution. The IP had to intervene and direct the go-around.
texts.1: SP recognised that the pattern being flown ahead was not correct but continued to follow it instead of calling for a go-around. The aircraft was held at the limit of the pattern parameters and the go-around was initiated only after the IP directed it. SP had no decision point in mind for breaking out of the pattern.
texts.2: SP followed the degraded pattern longer than necessary before reacting, so the deviation had already built up before the correction was made. The parameters remained inside the permitted band and SP decided in time to stop following the leader's track, re-established the correct pattern geometry and completed the approach without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP assessed the pattern being flown ahead against the briefed parameters and did not follow it when it degraded, flying his own correct pattern instead. All pattern parameters were held inside the required limits and the decision to correct rather than to follow was made early and stated clearly.
texts.4: SP continuously compared the pattern ahead with the briefed geometry, refused to follow the degraded track from the outset and flew a pattern with negligible deviations. The decision was made early, communicated without prompting and the go-around option was kept available throughout.
texts.marginal: SP did not follow the degraded pattern to the point of exceeding any limit, but this axis was marginal: the decision to stop matching the leader's track was taken late on each occasion and the parameters were allowed to reach the edge of the tolerance first. The go-around was treated as a last option rather than as a planned one. SP is expected to set a decision point in advance and to break out of a poorly flown pattern early, going around if required.

texts_at.1: SP initiated the go-around once the IP had directed it, the pattern parameters having been held at the limit before the decision was made. The delayed decision traced to no personal decision point being set for breaking out of a poorly flown pattern. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set a personal decision point for breaking out of a poorly flown pattern, before every recovery, not decide reactively at the limit.
texts_at.2: SP decided in time to stop following the leader's track, re-established the correct pattern geometry and completed the approach without IP intervention, the deviation held inside the permitted band throughout. The late reaction traced to the degraded pattern being followed longer than necessary before the correction was made. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to compare the pattern ahead against the briefed parameters continuously, not only once a deviation has already built up.
texts_at.3: SP assessed the pattern being flown ahead against the briefed parameters and did not follow it when it degraded, flying a correct pattern instead, all parameters held inside the required limits. The small residual came from the decision to correct stated a moment after it was made rather than at the same moment. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to state the decision to correct at the moment it is made, not a moment after.

texts_above.2: SP compared the pattern ahead against the briefed parameters continuously and stopped following it at the first sign of degradation, re-establishing correct geometry well inside the permitted band. Comparing that pattern continuously, from the outset, would remove the late reaction entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid go-around judgment.
texts_above.3: SP assessed the pattern being flown ahead against the briefed parameters and did not follow it when it degraded, flying a correct pattern instead, all pattern parameters held inside the required limits, the decision to correct made early and stated clearly. The technique is already sound; only the earliest sign of degradation still calls for the assessment to be a shade quicker. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate go-around judgment.
texts_above.4: SP continuously compared the pattern ahead with the briefed geometry, refused to follow the degraded track from the outset and flew a pattern with negligible deviations, the decision made early and communicated without prompting. The only refinement available was to log the decision point used for the debrief, since the judgment itself needed nothing further. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding go-around judgment.
